why_this_tool: OWASP ASVS gives a regulated customer's reviewer a list of verifiable application security requirements, and the OWASP threat modeling process is the laptop-only way to decide which of those requirements your AI deployment must meet and to prove it.
alternatives: NIST SP 800-53 is a broad control catalog for whole organisations and federal systems rather than a testable application checklist; OWASP Threat Dragon is a diagramming tool that draws and stores the threat model but does not supply requirements; Open Policy Agent enforces access rules as code at run time instead of documenting them; Presidio detects and masks PII in text but covers only that one control; Vault and cloud key management services hold keys and secrets and are evidence for a control, not the framework itself.

setup.do: Read the introduction to the OWASP threat modeling process and note the four steps it follows.
setup.done_when: You can name the four steps from memory and say what each one produces.
setup.why: The whole path follows these four steps, and the ASVS requirements you pick later only make sense once threats are identified this way.

setup.do: Create a local version-controlled folder for the review pack and choose one sample AI deployment to model, such as a retrieval assistant that answers questions over customer records containing PII and card data.
setup.done_when: The folder exists with a one-paragraph scope note that names the system, its users and what is out of scope.
setup.why: Scoping one concrete system keeps every later artifact specific. A folder under version control lets the model be reviewed and repeated like code.

setup.do: Install any free diagramming tool on your laptop and read the data flow diagram symbols the process uses.
setup.done_when: You can draw and label a process, a data store, a data flow and a trust boundary in your tool.
setup.why: Every later step refers to the processes, data stores, flows and trust boundaries on this diagram, so you need the notation before you draw.

steps.do: Write the threat model information header for your sample deployment: application name, version, description, document owner, participants and reviewer.
steps.done_when: A header file in your folder has every field from the sample filled in for your deployment.
steps.why: This is the first artifact a customer reviewer reads. It fixes exactly which version of the system the review covers.

steps.do: Create the external dependencies table, listing the model endpoint, the vector index, the identity provider, the key manager and the logging store.
steps.done_when: Each dependency has an ID and a description stating what your system assumes about it.
steps.why: In an AI deployment most of the risk sits in components you do not own. Reviewers ask about each of them by name.

steps.do: Write the entry points table, covering the chat interface, the document ingestion job, the retrieval query path, tool calls and the admin console.
steps.done_when: Every way data or instructions can enter the system has an ID, a description and the trust levels allowed to use it.
steps.why: Entry points are where an attacker reaches the system. For an AI system they include prompts and ingested documents, not only web endpoints.

steps.do: Create the assets table, listing raw PII and payment data, then the derived data: embeddings, index entries, prompt and response logs, caches and evaluation sets.
steps.done_when: Each derived data item appears as its own asset with an ID and a note saying which source data it was built from.
steps.why: Derived data carries the same regulated content as its source and is the part teams forget. It must be a named asset before it can be governed.

steps.do: Write the trust levels table, then record for each derived data asset which trust level may read it, how long it is kept and how it is deleted when the source record is removed.
steps.done_when: Every derived data asset has an access rule, a retention period and a deletion path written next to it, with no blank cells.
steps.why: Governance of retention, deletion and access is only reviewable when each rule is tied to a named asset and a named trust level.

steps.do: Create the data flow diagram for the deployment, drawing trust boundaries around the customer network, your application, the model endpoint and the index.
steps.done_when: Every entry point, asset and external dependency from your tables appears on the diagram, and each flow carrying PII or card data is labelled.
steps.why: The diagram shows where regulated data crosses a boundary inside a prompt or an index write. Those crossings are where controls are needed.

steps.do: Run a STRIDE pass over every element and boundary crossing on the diagram, adding AI cases such as prompt injection through ingested documents and leakage of another user's records through retrieval.
steps.done_when: A threat list exists where each threat has an ID, a STRIDE category, and the diagram element and asset it affects.
steps.why: Walking the six categories element by element is what makes a threat model complete rather than a list of the threats you happened to think of.

steps.do: Compare the threats with the qualitative risk model and rank them, scoring likelihood and impact for each.
steps.done_when: Every threat has a risk rating and the list is sorted with the top five clearly marked.
steps.why: A reviewer wants to see that the highest risks got controls first. The ranking also tells you which ASVS requirements are mandatory for this deployment.

steps.do: Write a countermeasure for each ranked threat using the STRIDE mitigation techniques, then map each one to the matching OWASP ASVS requirement and the matching NIST SP 800-53 control family in two extra columns.
steps.done_when: No ranked threat is without a countermeasure, and each countermeasure names one ASVS requirement and one NIST SP 800-53 family.
steps.why: Regulated customers ask in the language of their control framework. A mapping from threat to control to requirement lets them tick off their checklist quickly.

steps.do: Write the data protection countermeasures for each flow labelled as PII or card data: encryption in transit and at rest with a named key owner, and masking or tokenising of values before they reach a prompt, a log or the index.
steps.done_when: Each labelled flow on the diagram has an encryption control and a masking decision recorded, with each threat marked mitigated, partially mitigated or not mitigated.
steps.why: Information disclosure threats against regulated data are closed by encryption and masking. The reviewer needs to see which control sits on which flow.

steps.do: Reproduce the assessment from scratch after changing one thing in the design, such as adding a new tool call, and configure a checklist in the repository that must be completed on every design change.
steps.done_when: The repository history shows a second pass with updated tables and diagram, and a checklist file lists the checks to repeat on each change.
steps.why: A threat model that is not rerun on change goes stale. A repeatable assessment step is what turns it into a standing control rather than a one-off document.

steps.do: Package the review pack as you would hand it to a customer security team: scope, diagram, asset and trust tables, ranked threats, the control mapping and the open risks, then use it to direct a code review of the highest-risk entry points.
steps.done_when: A single document in the folder lets a colleague acting as reviewer trace any top threat to its control, its ASVS requirement and the code area to inspect, without asking you a question.
steps.why: This is the production-like end state. A complete pack that already links threats to code and controls is what makes a customer security review go quickly.
